content: 1. Ritonavir is abbreviated as RTV. 2. Dolutegravir is abbreviated as DTG. 3. Efavirenz is abbreviated as EFV. 4. Emtricitabine is abbreviated as FTC. 5. Lopinavir/ritonavir is abbreviated as LPV/r. 6. Nevirapine is abbreviated as NVP. 7. Raltegravir is abbreviated as RAL. 8. Tenofovir alafenamide is abbreviated as TAF. 9. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is abbreviated as TDF. 10. Tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in children and adolescents living with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART) presents challenges, particularly due to drug-drug interactions with rifamycin-based regimens. 11. Rifampicin and rifapentine can be co-administered with efavirenz (EFV) or dolutegravir (DTG) without requiring dose adjustments. 12. For individuals on raltegravir (RAL) and rifamycins, the RAL dosage should be increased to 800 mg twice daily instead of the standard 400 mg twice daily. This adjustment is applicable only to adolescents, as pharmacokinetic studies on the use of 3HP, 1HP, and 3HR in children on newer ART regimens are ongoing. 13. Rifampicin or rifapentine-based TPT regimens should not be co-administered with protease inhibitors (PIs) or nevirapine (NVP). 14. Further details on drug-drug interactions between TPT and ART medications are available in Chapter 6 of the WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis, Module 1: Prevention – Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment. 15. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), also known as a paradoxical reaction, is a temporary clinical deterioration that may occur within three months of initiating ART, most commonly within the first month. 16. As the immune system begins to recover after ART initiation, CD4 counts increase, and viral loads are suppressed. This immune reconstitution in response to mycobacterial antigens can trigger an inflammatory reaction to tuberculosis (TB) antigens at the sites of TB disease. 17. IRIS can manifest as either a worsening of a treated infection or the emergence of a previously subclinical infection. 18. Risk factors for IRIS include low baseline CD4 counts, extensive or disseminated TB, early initiation of ART, and rapid immunological and virological responses to ART. 19. TB-IRIS and BCG-IRIS are significant causes of morbidity but are not associated with increased mortality risk. 20. While IRIS following BCG immunization is frequently reported in children, paradoxical and unmasking TB-IRIS are less well-documented in children compared to adults, largely due to the challenges in diagnosing TB in children living with HIV. 21. TB-IRIS in children is often a diagnosis of exclusion. 22. There are two main presentations of TB-IRIS: Exacerbation of known TB disease in a child or adolescent living with HIV on TB treatment who is starting ART (paradoxical TB-IRIS). Development of TB disease in a child or adolescent living with HIV starting ART (unmasking TB-IRIS). 23. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be prescribed to children or adolescents with clinical deterioration after starting ART if a bacterial infection is considered in the differential diagnosis. 24. In most cases, it is safe to continue TB treatment and ART. 25. Temporarily stopping ART should be considered if TB-IRIS is life-threatening or likely to cause permanent disability. 26. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be considered for mild to moderate TB-IRIS. 27. Corticosteroids may be considered for severe TB-IRIS but should not be used if drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) is a likely diagnosis. 28. If there is uncertainty about the diagnosis or management, the child should be referred to the next level of care. 29. TB in pregnancy contributes to 6–15% of all maternal mortality and is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, vaginal bleeding, hospitalization, and miscarriage. 30. Perinatal outcomes include a two-fold increased risk of premature birth, low birth weight, and intrauterine growth retardation, as well as a six-fold increased risk of perinatal death. 31. Maternal TB more than doubles the risk of vertical transmission of HIV and increases mortality risk in newborns and other young children in the household. 32. The increase in TB incidence in the postpartum period is likely due to delays in early detection during pregnancy, resulting from physiological and immunological changes. 33. Symptoms of TB disease in pregnancy are similar to those in non-pregnant women, but pregnancy may mask true weight loss. Failure to gain weight is an important symptom to consider. 34. Pulmonary TB (PTB) is the most common form of TB disease in pregnancy. Disseminated TB occurs in 5–10% of pregnant women with TB disease and poses a particular risk for congenital TB in newborns. 35. All pregnant women in TB and HIV-endemic regions should be screened for TB symptoms. Pregnant women with presumptive TB should also be tested for HIV. 36. TB treatment in pregnant women is the same as for non-pregnant women. 37. All pregnant women with TB/HIV co-infection are eligible for ART and should be treated according to the most recent WHO guidelines. 38. Congenital TB is acquired in utero through hematogenous spread via the umbilical cord or during delivery through aspiration or ingestion of infected amniotic fluid or cervicovaginal secretions. It usually presents within the first three weeks of life and has a high mortality rate. 39. Neonatal TB is acquired after birth through exposure to a person with infectious TB, usually the mother or another close contact. 40. It is often difficult to distinguish between congenital and neonatal TB, but management is the same. 41. Neonates exposed to TB may be asymptomatic or symptomatic. Symptoms of neonatal TB are usually non-specific and include lethargy, fever, poor feeding, low birth weight, and poor weight gain. Clinical signs are also non-specific and include respiratory distress, non-resolving pneumonia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, abdominal distension with ascites, and a clinical picture of neonatal sepsis with disseminated TB. 42. The diagnosis of TB should be included in the differential diagnosis of chronic neonatal infection with a poor response to antimicrobial therapy. 43. The most important pointer to the diagnosis of neonatal TB is a maternal history of TB disease or HIV infection. 44. Treatment of congenital and neonatal TB is the same and should be managed by a clinician experienced in pediatric TB. 45. A complete investigation of the mother and neonate should be undertaken, including chest X-rays and appropriate specimen collection for diagnostic confirmation. 46. Treatment should be initiated based on the likelihood of TB, even before bacteriological confirmation, as TB can progress rapidly in neonates. 47. Dosage adjustments may be required to account for age and potential toxicity in young infants. 48. WHO recommendations on treatment for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) apply to neonates as well. 49. Breastfeeding is recommended regardless of the mother's TB status, as the risk of TB transmission through breast milk is negligible. 50. Separation from the mother is not advised, especially in resource-limited settings where breastfeeding is critical for the child's survival. 51. Asymptomatic neonates born to women with presumptive or confirmed TB should be screened for TB disease. If there is no evidence of TB disease, preventive treatment should be provided, and BCG vaccination should be delayed until after completion of TPT. 52. Neonates born to women with MDR/RR-TB should be referred to a local expert in pediatric MDR/RR-TB management. 53. Infection control measures, such as wearing masks, are required to reduce the likelihood of transmission to the neonate.
